title: AI for Formulas
goal: Ask an AI for a formula, test it on a case you can count, read what it does, and fix it when it's wrong.

steps.text:
AI tools are good at three formula jobs: **generate** one from plain English, **explain** one you don't understand, and **fix** one that's broken. They also write formulas that look perfect and aren't.

So the loop is always the same:
• Ask, and give your column letters
• Paste the reply into **one cell**
• **Test it** on a case you can count by hand
• Only then fill it down

Here's a marks sheet. An AI will suggest formulas for it, and you'll be the checker.

steps.topic: Test a reply you can count
steps.prompt:
You asked an AI: “How many students scored **40 or more** in Maths (column B)?” It replied with `=COUNTIF(B2:B7,">=40")`.

Type that into ==B8==, then check it by eye: which marks are 40 or more?
steps.explain: **4**: Asha 72, Bilal 40, Divya 58 and Farah 91. You counted four by eye and the formula agrees, so this one is safe to trust. That's the habit: test on a case you can count.

wrongFeedback.missingFunction: Counting with a test is a job for `COUNTIF`.
wrongFeedback.wrongValue: It should give 4. Check the quotes and the `>=`: `">=40"`.

steps.prompt:
Now Science (column C). The AI replied `=COUNTIF(C2:C7,">40")`. By eye, five students scored 40 or more in Science, so something's off.

Type the corrected formula in ==C8==.
steps.explain: **5.** The AI's version gave 3: `>40` skips students on exactly 40, and Chen and Farah both have 40. “40 or more” needs `>=`. Always test with a value that sits on the boundary.

wrongFeedback.wrongValue: Two students scored exactly 40 in Science. “40 or more” includes them, so use `>=`.

steps.prompt:
For a new question, the AI suggests `=SUMIF(B2:B7,">=40",C2:C7)`.

Read it as “where column B is 40 or more, add column C”. Before you try it: what will it return?
options: `185`, Science marks of students who passed Maths
`4`, the number of students who passed Maths
steps.explain: Maths passes are Asha, Bilal, Divya and Farah. Their Science marks: 45 + 62 + 38 + 40 = **185**. Reading a formula aloud like this is also how you check an AI's explanation of it.
wrongFeedback: 280 is everyone's Science marks. The test on column B filters out Chen and Eshan.
4 is how many passed. `SUMIF` adds the marks in column C, it doesn't count.
clues: Which rows have Maths of 40 or more? Add their Science marks.

steps.prompt: Now prove your prediction. Type the AI's formula in ==D2==.
steps.explain: **185.** Your prediction held, so you understood the formula before trusting it. If a prediction and the result ever disagree, one of you misread something: find out which.

wrongFeedback.missingFunction: Add values that pass a test with `SUMIF`.
wrongFeedback.wrongValue: Use the test on column B (`B2:B7`) and add column C (`C2:C7`).

steps.prompt:
You asked an AI for the price of the ID in `E2`. It replied `=XLOOKUP(E2,A2:A5,C3:C6)`, and Tea shows **25**, but Tea costs 20.

What's wrong? Type the corrected formula in ==F2==.
steps.explain: **20.** The AI looked in `A2:A5` but returned from `C3:C6`: one row lower, so every answer was shifted (Tea's 3rd row gave Samosa's 25). The two ranges must start and end on the same rows.

wrongFeedback.missingFunction: Keep it a lookup with `XLOOKUP`: just fix the return range.
wrongFeedback.wrongValue: The ranges must line up: IDs in `A2:A5` and prices in `C2:C5`, both starting on row 2.

clues: Compare the first row of each range: `A2` and `C3`.

steps.prompt: You paste an AI formula, `=SUMIFTEXT(B2:B9,"Pune")`, and the cell shows `#NAME?`. What's the most likely cause?
options: Excel doesn't know that function name
The numbers are stored as text
steps.explain: `#NAME?` means Excel doesn't recognise a name. AI tools sometimes **invent** function names that sound right (`SUMIFTEXT` doesn't exist) or use ones newer than your Excel. Look the name up in Excel's help, or ask for another way using a function you can find there.
wrongFeedback: A missing item would give `0` or `#N/A`, not `#NAME?`.
Text-numbers give a wrong total (often 0), not `#NAME?`.
clues: `#NAME?` is about a **name** Excel can't find.

steps.prompt:
The AI wrote `=B2*E2` for the tax, with the 5% rate in `E2`. Row 2 worked, but after you filled it down, rows 3 and 4 show **0**.

What fixes it?
options: Type the rate again in `E3` and `E4`
steps.explain: `E2` is **relative**: filled down, it slid to `E3`, which is empty, so the tax became 0. `$E$2` is **absolute** and never moves. Watch for this whenever one cell (a rate, a limit) feeds many rows.
wrongFeedback: That would work today, but you'd have to repeat it for every row and change 100 cells when the rate changes.
That leaves rows 3 and 4 with no tax at all. You want one formula that works in every row.
clues: Which part of the formula should stay put when it's copied down?

steps.prompt:
You pasted an AI formula over the Bonus column, and every bonus turned into 0. Before you do anything else, press [[Ctrl]] + [[Z]] to undo.

Tip: try AI formulas on a **copy** of your sheet or in a spare column first.
clues: Hold Ctrl and tap Z. Mac: Cmd + Z.

steps.prompt:
You asked an AI to explain what a formula should do. It wrote: “Show **Pass** if **both** the Maths and Science marks are 40 or more, otherwise show **Fail**.”

Build that formula for Gita's row, in ==D2==.
steps.explain: `Fail`: Gita's Maths 40 passes but Science 38 doesn't, and “both” needs both. If a formula used `OR` instead of `AND`, it would say Pass here. Turning an explanation back into a formula shows whether you really understood it.

wrongFeedback.missingReference: Both marks matter: your formula must look at `B2` (Maths) and `C2` (Science).
wrongFeedback.wrongValue: Gita passes Maths but not Science, so “both” isn't true: the answer is Fail.

steps.prompt:
An AI wrote the weekly total in an earlier version of this sheet. It stopped at Friday and said **600**. Saturday's 200 has been added since.

Put the total for the whole week in ==B8==.
steps.explain: **800.** The old formula's range ended one row too early, a classic slip when rows are added. Whenever data grows, check that totals still reach the last row.

wrongFeedback.missingFunction: Add the whole column of daily sales with `SUM`.

clues: Cover Monday to Saturday: `B2` down to `B7`.
